analysis.one_liner: Blocks imported ethanol from counting toward any future renewable fuel mandate.
analysis.headline: The bill to keep imported ethanol out of a future renewable fuel mandate never received a committee hearing and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written one rule into law ahead of time: if Congress ever created a renewable fuel standard — a requirement that motor fuel contain a set share of ethanol or other renewable fuel — only ethanol produced in the United States could be used to meet it. Ethanol imported from abroad, or made from imported material, would not count. The practical effect would be to guarantee the entire mandated market to domestic ethanol producers, most of whom make ethanol from corn, and to shut out cheaper foreign ethanol, mainly Brazilian sugarcane ethanol. The bill never got a committee hearing and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic ethanol producers and the corn growers who supply them would gain the most: the bill would guarantee that any future federal renewable fuel mandate could be satisfied only with American-made ethanol, locking in demand for their product and eliminating competition from cheaper Brazilian sugarcane ethanol. Supporters framed this as protecting US energy security and Midwest jobs, since the mandated market would be built entirely at home rather than partly met by imports.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic ethanol producers and corn growers

how_it_helps.text: It would guarantee domestic ethanol producers the entire compliance market under any future renewable fuel standard, since imported ethanol and ethanol made from imported material could not be used to meet it.
It was designed to apply to a standard that Congress had not yet enacted, so it would have shaped whatever mandate Congress later wrote to exclude foreign supply from day one.
Supporters, all from ethanol-producing Midwestern states, presented it as a way to ensure a renewable fuel requirement builds domestic production and energy security.

analysis.who_pays: Fuel refiners and blenders would pay higher compliance costs, since they could not meet the mandate with the lowest-priced ethanol available and would have to buy domestic supply — costs that generally pass through to prices at the pump. Foreign ethanol producers, chiefly in Brazil, would be shut out of the market entirely, and drivers would forgo the price competition their cheaper product would have provided.

drawbacks.text: The bill was written before any renewable fuel standard existed, and it would have foreclosed a decision in advance: whatever mandate Congress later wrote, imports would be barred from counting toward it, removing the option of using cheaper foreign ethanol.

Excluding imports would raise compliance costs for refiners and blenders, who would be required to buy domestic ethanol rather than the lowest-priced supply; those costs generally flow to fuel prices.

A good-faith objection from the other side: Brazilian sugarcane ethanol is generally cheaper and yields more energy per unit of input than corn ethanol, so a domestic-only rule would push the mandate toward the more expensive and less efficient product, which supporters of free trade and of cheaper fuel would oppose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — guaranteed demand for domestic ethanol and corn — flows to a specific Midwestern industry, not to the public broadly. Its cost — foreclosing cheaper imported ethanol from any future mandate — would fall on refiners and ultimately on drivers, and it would remove the pressure that foreign competition puts on domestic producers to improve efficiency. The energy-security argument has some force, but the bill was written defensively, before any standard existed, and with no analysis in the record of what the restriction would cost. On balance it reads as a protective measure for one industry rather than a policy with public benefits that outweigh its public costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no further action until Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Daschle introduced the bill on July 22, 2004, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee the same day.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, which killed the bill under congressional rules.
No vote was ever held on the bill in either chamber, despite its bipartisan sponsorship from three Republicans and two Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Imported ethanol suppliers and refiners who wanted the option of cheaper foreign ethanol were better off because the restriction never took effect. The domestic ethanol industry lost little in practice, since Congress went on to enact a renewable fuel mandate in the Energy Policy Act of 2005 without an import ban.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Importers and refiners using cheaper ethanol

for.name: Sen. Thomas Daschle
for.role: Senator from South Dakota and Senate Democratic Leader; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat and three of his four cosponsors were from the opposing party — two Republicans and one Democrat, all from ethanol-producing Midwestern states; no one ever voted on or against the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have locked domestic ethanol in as the only commodity that could satisfy any future federal renewable fuel mandate, making producers the permanent, protected channel for compliance. That protection would come at the expense of cheaper imported ethanol that refiners could otherwise use.

A domestic-only mandate would raise demand for corn as the feedstock for nearly all US ethanol, supporting farm prices in corn-growing states. The benefit is concentrated among growers rather than spread across the public.

industries.industry: Foreign ethanol producers (notably Brazilian sugarcane ethanol exporters)
industries.note: The bill would have shut foreign ethanol out of the compliance market entirely regardless of price or quality. Foreign producers' ability to offer cheaper ethanol is the same option that would have held costs down for refiners and drivers.

The bill would have removed their flexibility to meet a federal fuel mandate with the lowest-cost ethanol available, forcing them to buy domestic supply. Higher compliance costs of this kind generally pass through to fuel prices.
